catalog_locator: sec. 2.8 'Tone inventory', preprint pp. 6-7 (text extraction); sec. 3.2.3 'Tone', preprint p. 12.
catalog_quote: Wanga has two surface tones, High (H) and Low (L), but presents evidence for a three-way underlying tonal contrast: /H/, /L/, and /Ø/ (toneless). Tones associate with the mora as tone bearing unit (TBU). Evidence for the mora is clearest from tone spreading processes like Melodic Doubling where a Melodic H tone spreads rightward by one mora. ... Most phonetic L tones arise on /Ø/ TBUs, with L inserted by default. However, underlying /L/ is found with some noun tone melodies, the reflexive object marker, and one tonal class of verb roots (historically *H roots synchronically have initial /L/). Ls block H tone assignment (6) and anticipatory tone spreading (7). Toneless TBUs are transparent to these processes. ... [sec. 3.2.3 Tone:] Wanga verbs fall into two lexical tone classes: oxú[βál-á] ‘to count’ vs. oxu[βáꜜl-á] ‘to get warm (e.g. water).’ The first class corresponds to historically *Ø verbs, and the second class corresponds to historically *H verbs.
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wanga is described purely as a tone language: surface H vs L, underlying three-way /H/ vs /L/ vs toneless, mora as TBU, lexical tone classes in nouns (8+ surface patterns) and verb roots (two classes) plus melodic (grammatical) H tones. The sketch's phonology section (vowels with length contrast neutralized word-initially/finally, open syllables, tone) contains no statement about word stress, accent or prominence, and no mention of penultimate lengthening. Corroborated first-hand by Akidah 2000 p.8 ('Luwanga like all its sister dialects of Luhya.. is tonal'; suprasegmentals excluded) and Ebarb, Green & Marlo 2014 p.135 ('Wanga is a central Luyia variety with a reversive tonal system').
new_statements.exceptions: none (no stress statement to qualify); vowel length contrast is neutralized to short word-initially and word-finally (sec. 2.1)
new_statements.domain_note: Tone described for words in isolation and in phrasal contexts (HTA, HTI, phrase-medial H deletion); sentence-level tone explicitly still under study (fn. to sec. 4). No word-stress domain discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Wanga proper (Luwanga/Oluwanga, iso lwg = wang1294), spoken around Mumias/Matungu, Kakamega County. Green et al.'s data come mainly from consultant Alfred Anangwe and fieldwork 2006-2018; Green & Farris-Trimble's speaker is from Musamba; Mukanda's speakers from Matungu; Akidah's from Mumias. No dialect mismatch.

tone_statements.citation: Marlo, Michael R. 2013. Verb tone in Bantu languages: micro-typological patterns and research methods. Africana Linguistica 19: 137-234. doi:10.3406/aflin.2013.1020
tone_statements.quote: reversive systems maintain a contrast between two tonal types of verb roots, but like predictable systems, all verbal contexts are marked with an inflectional tone. … a second possible type of reversive system within Bantu inverts a historical contrast between * H and * Ø roots as a synchronic contrast between / L/ and / Ø/. The varieties of central Luyia Bukusu (Austen 1974, Mutonyi 2000), one variety of Marachi (Marlo 2007), and Wanga (Green & Marlo 2013) can be characterized as having this kind of reversive system, though not all researchers agree on the / L/ vs. / Ø/ analysis.

tone_statements.summary: Classed as a 'reversive' verb-tone system (after Green & Marlo 2013): verb roots contrast lexical /L/ vs toneless /Ø/ (< *H vs *Ø); every verb form carries an inflectional tone; no tone count given.
